8 Changes to materials

8.1 Simple chemical reactions

Key words: chemical reaction · combine · product · react · reactant

Physical properties and chemical properties

The physical properties of a substance are features such as:

  • what colour it is
  • whether it is a solid, a liquid or a gas
  • what its boiling or melting temperature is
  • whether it is heavy or light.

For example, some of the physical properties of iron are that it is a grey, heavy solid with a melting point of 1538 °C. One of the physical properties of hydrochloric acid is that it is a colourless liquid.

The chemical properties of a substance are features such as:

  • how acidic or alkaline it is
  • how it reacts with water, acids or metals
  • how readily it reacts.

Some of the chemical properties of iron are that it combines with sulfur when heated to form iron sulfide, and that it combines with oxygen to form iron oxide (rust). One of the chemical properties of hydrochloric acid is that it has a pH of 2.

Physical changes and chemical changes

In a physical change, no new substances are formed. When liquid water freezes, the water has changed state but it is still the same substance after the change.

In a chemical change, new substances are formed. When iron and sulfur are heated together, they form a new substance — a compound called iron sulfide.

iron + sulfur → iron sulfide

The iron and the sulfur have reacted together to form a new substance, so a chemical reaction has taken place. The iron atoms have combined and bonded with the sulfur atoms.

  • The reactants are the substances that react together — here, iron and sulfur.
  • The products are the new substances made in the reaction — here, there is only one product, iron sulfide.

In some chemical reactions a substance breaks apart to make new substances. Water, for example, can be split apart to form oxygen and hydrogen.

water → oxygen + hydrogen

Chemical reactions happen everywhere: inside plants when they grow and when they decay, and inside your body to keep you alive — for example when you digest food.

Burning

Burning is a chemical reaction. When a substance burns, it reacts with the oxygen in the air. Sometimes ashes are formed, and the new substances in the ashes are oxides.

Charcoal is made of the element carbon. When carbon burns it combines with oxygen in the air to make the gas carbon dioxide.

carbon + oxygen → carbon dioxide

When magnesium metal is burnt, a white powder is formed. This powder is magnesium oxide. Magnesium and oxygen are the reactants; magnesium oxide is the product. A chemical property of magnesium is that it burns in air to form magnesium oxide by combining with oxygen.

magnesium + oxygen → magnesium oxide

Comparing the properties of reactants and products

The properties of a product are different from the properties of the reactants it was made from.

Reactant: magnesiumReactant: oxygenProduct: magnesium oxide
Element or compound?elementelementcompound
State at room temperaturesolidgassolid
Appearancesoft, shiny, malleablecolourless, no smellwhite, powdery
Conducts electricity?yesnono
Melting point in °C651−2142800

Reactions with water

Some substances react very violently with water; some do not react with water at all.

Potassium is a metal that is so soft it can be cut with a knife — that is a physical property. Potassium is so reactive that it has to be stored under oil to stop it reacting with the water vapour in the air — that is a chemical property.

When a very small piece of potassium is placed in a large trough of water, hydrogen gas is given off. The reaction produces so much heat that the gas burns.

Safety: you cannot carry out the potassium and water reaction yourself. If your teacher shows it as a demonstration, you must wear safety glasses and there must be a safety screen in front of the trough.

Reactions with acid

When magnesium is placed in hydrochloric acid, bubbles of gas are given off. The magnesium has reacted with the acid and formed new substances: the gas is hydrogen, and magnesium chloride is also formed.

magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

When you see bubbles forming in a reaction you know a gas is being produced — but you cannot tell which gas it is without a test.

Testing for hydrogen

Hydrogen gas burns with a squeaky pop. To carry out the test you light a splint and place it in the mouth of the test tube. Keep your finger over the end of the test tube until the last moment, or there will be no hydrogen left to test, because hydrogen gas is lighter than air.

When the hydrogen pops, it is reacting with oxygen in the air to form water.

Collecting hydrogen over water

Hydrogen can be produced on a larger scale by collecting the gas over water. The acid is poured in through the thistle funnel onto the metal in the conical flask. The gas travels along the delivery tube, bubbles up under the bee-hive shelf and pushes the water out of the measuring cylinder, so the volume of gas can be measured.

Questions from the book — 8.1
  1. Compare the melting points of magnesium, oxygen and magnesium oxide. The melting point of magnesium is 651 °C and that of oxygen is −214 °C, whereas the melting point of the product, magnesium oxide, is much higher at 2800 °C.
  2. Find one similarity between magnesium oxide and one of the reactants. Both magnesium and magnesium oxide are solids.
  3. Physical change or chemical reaction? a Making toast — chemical reaction. b Melting chocolate — physical change. c Fireworks going off — chemical reaction. d Ice melting — physical change. e Coal burning — chemical reaction. f Copper roof turning green — chemical reaction.
  4. Give two chemical properties of magnesium. Magnesium reacts with oxygen to produce magnesium oxide, and it reacts with hydrochloric acid to produce magnesium chloride and hydrogen.
  5. Give two physical properties of magnesium. Magnesium is a light grey/silver coloured solid which is readily malleable. (Other properties, such as being very light or soft, are also acceptable.)
  6. What are the products when zinc reacts with hydrochloric acid? Zinc chloride and hydrogen.
Getting started — hazard symbols
  • A substance that can poison you: toxic
  • A substance that catches fire easily: flammable
  • A substance that can dissolve your skin: corrosive
Think like a scientist — burning magnesium

You hold a piece of magnesium ribbon in tongs and put it into a Bunsen flame.

  1. Describe what happens to the magnesium ribbon. It burns very brightly, and the ribbon disappears (changes).
  2. Describe what has been formed. A white powder is formed.
  3. Name the reactants. The reactants are magnesium and oxygen.
  4. Safety precautions. Wear safety glasses; do not look directly at the burning magnesium; hold the magnesium at arm's length; take care with the hot tongs.

Not all metals have the same chemical properties as magnesium — they may not burn in the same way. You could try holding pieces of copper, zinc or iron in the Bunsen flame and record what happens.

Think like a scientist — reactions with water and acid

Part 1: put a small piece of each metal into a different test tube, add water until the tube is half full, and record your observations in a table. Part 2: repeat with hydrochloric acid instead of water; if bubbles are given off, test for hydrogen.

  1. Write the reactants and products for each reaction with acid. Each reaction should show the relevant reactants and products — for example, reactants: zinc and hydrochloric acid; products: zinc chloride and hydrogen. Where there was no reaction, write only the names of the reactants, because no new products were made.
  2. Safety precautions. Wear safety glasses; handle acid with care; do not overfill the test tubes, to avoid fizzing and spilling.
  3. How did you test for hydrogen? A lighted splint placed in the mouth of a test tube containing hydrogen will produce a pop sound.

8.2 Neutralisation

Key words: burette · decay · digest · filtrate · indigestion · neutralisation · neutralised

Mixing acids and alkalis

Acids and alkalis can cancel each other out. When you mix them together they react and make a neutral solution. This is called neutralisation, and it is another chemical change. Neutrality is also a chemical property of a substance.

  • Add too much acid to an alkali and you make an acidic liquid.
  • Add too little acid and the liquid stays alkaline.

Adding the acid very slowly, a few drops at a time, makes it easier to judge exactly when the mixture becomes neutral.

Making a neutral solution with a burette

You can use a piece of equipment called a burette to neutralise an alkali very accurately. Universal indicator is added to the alkali in the conical flask, and acid is run in from the burette.

StageVolume of acid addedpH in the flaskWhat it means
At the start0 cm³about 13strongly alkaline
Part way25 cm³7neutral — the acid has neutralised the alkali
A little more acidmore than 25 cm³about 6weakly acidic

The flask is shaken each time some acid is added. A chemical reaction takes place and new substances are formed. With hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide (an alkali) as the reactants, the products are sodium chloride and water.

hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water

Neutralisation in everyday life

Indigestion. Your stomach produces hydrochloric acid, which gives the stomach the right conditions to digest your food. When your stomach produces too much acid you get indigestion, which can be very uncomfortable. The medicines that help are all alkalis that neutralise the acid; they are sometimes called antacids.

Toothpaste. There are millions of bacteria in your mouth. They feed on pieces of food left on your teeth, and they produce acid when they feed. This acid damages your teeth and makes them decay. Toothpaste contains alkali, which helps to neutralise the acid.

Neutralising lakes. In some parts of the world, harmful chemicals in the air make the rain acidic. This acid rain damages trees and changes the pH of lakes, rivers and ponds. The plants and animals that live there cannot survive in acid conditions, so some countries drop alkalis into the lakes to neutralise the acid.

Growing crops. In some areas the soil is very acidic and plants do not grow well. Farmers spread lime on the soil to neutralise the acid so the plants grow better.

Questions from the book — 8.2
  1. What colour is universal indicator when the solution is neutral? Green.
  2. What sort of reaction happens when an acid and an alkali are mixed? A neutralisation reaction.
  3. Why is toothpaste alkaline? So that it can neutralise the acid in your mouth and help to stop your teeth decaying.
  4. Where does the acid in your mouth come from? From the millions of bacteria there. When the bacteria feed, they produce acid.
  5. Why is an alkaline substance dropped into lakes in some countries? The lakes have become very acidic as a result of acid rain. This changes the pH so that plants and animals can no longer live there, and the alkali overcomes this.
  6. What do farmers spread onto acidic soil, and why? Lime. It neutralises the acid, so that crops which prefer less acidic soil will grow well.
Activity 8.2.1 — Rainbow neutralisation

A crystal of washing soda is put in the bottom of a clamped test tube, water is added until the tube is two-thirds full, universal indicator is added, and acid is poured carefully on top. The tube is left to stand for a few days without being moved.

  1. pH at the top of the tube? About pH 2 (it depends on how well the practical was carried out).
  2. pH at the bottom of the tube? About pH 13.
  3. The most alkaline part of the tube? The bottom of the test tube.
  4. Why must the tube be kept still? So that the liquids do not mix too much.
  5. Which hazard symbols were on the equipment? This depends on the acid and alkali used. Most likely corrosive (can destroy living tissue and cause burns) or health hazard (can cause harm and irritate skin and eyes).

How the rainbow appears. At the top, the acid turns the indicator red — strongly acidic; as the acid particles move down and mix with more water it turns yellow — weakly acidic. In the middle, the acid and washing soda solution meet and react, neutralising each other. At the bottom, the washing soda dissolves and the indicator turns purple or dark blue — strongly alkaline; further up it becomes lighter blue — weakly alkaline.

Think like a scientist — testing the pH of soil

Take a sample of soil in a test tube, add water and shake. Filter the mixture, then add a few drops of universal indicator to the filtrate (the liquid that comes through the filter paper), and record the result. The answer depends on your own soil sample.

  1. Read the measuring cylinders. B 25 cm³, C 36 cm³, D 12 cm³, E 47 cm³.
  2. Draw the liquid levels at: B 20 cm³, C 35 cm³, D 15 cm³, E 5 cm³. The lines should be slightly curved (a meniscus), with the bottom of the curve at the level of the scale reading.
  3. Read the burettes. A 16 cm³, B 23 cm³, C 40 cm³, D 49 cm³, E 62 cm³. (Remember that a burette scale is numbered from the top downwards.)
Workbook — Exercise 8.2B Neutralising acid

A model answer, written as a method:

I put on my safety glasses to protect my eyes in case of spills or splashes. I collected the chemicals from the teacher and used a beaker to take a small amount of acid back to my workspace. I used 0.5 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid and carefully filled a burette. I made sure the burette was secure in the clamp stand and that the tap was closed, so that no acid was spilt. I collected some sodium hydroxide from the teacher in a beaker. I measured 25 cm³ of the sodium hydroxide using a measuring cylinder and put it into a conical flask. I added a few drops of universal indicator solution; the solution turned blue because sodium hydroxide is an alkali. I placed the conical flask under the burette. I slowly added acid from the burette to the conical flask, gently shaking the flask each time I added acid, and watching the colour of the solution. When the solution was green, I knew I had added enough acid to neutralise the sodium hydroxide.

The important points are: the acid goes in the burette; the sodium hydroxide is measured with a measuring cylinder or pipette; and the safety measures are given together with the reasons for them.

8.3 Investigating acids and alkalis

Key words: remedy · variable

Asking questions you can answer

Scientists ask questions, then devise tests to look for the answers. Here are some questions about neutralisation that a scientist might try to answer.

  • How much lime should be added to an acid lake to neutralise it?
  • Which is the best indigestion remedy (treatment for an illness or injury)?
  • How much toothpaste is needed to neutralise the acid in your mouth?

'Which is the best indigestion remedy?' is not a precise question. What does best mean — the most pleasant tasting, the cheapest, the most effective, or the most cost-effective? A scientist would rewrite it so that it can be tested, for example:

Which indigestion powder neutralises the acid using the least amount of powder?

Planning an investigation

When you plan an investigation you have to design an experiment. If you are investigating the effect of indigestion powders on stomach acid, you cannot use your own stomach acid — you have to use a model instead, such as a beaker of acid.

There is a lot to think about:

  • What will I change, and what will I keep the same? The things that can change are called variables.
  • How will I make my test fair?
  • What will I measure, and how will I know when the powder has neutralised the acid?
  • What equipment do I need?
  • What will I do to stay safe?
  • How will I record the results?

Which powder is best at neutralising acid?

Marcus and Arun put 20 cm³ of hydrochloric acid into each of three beakers. The acid has a pH of 1, like the strong acid in your stomach. They put a few drops of universal indicator in each beaker, then added indigestion powder spatula by spatula until the indicator turned green, recording the number of spatulas used.

Their first set of results:

PowderNumber of spatulas used to neutralise the acid
A10
B6
C24

They then repeated the whole investigation twice more:

PowderFirst trySecond tryThird tryMean
A1091110
B6171613
C24232524

With only one set of results, powder B looked the most effective. With three sets, it is clear that B's first result was an anomaly, and powder A is really the most effective. This is why an investigation is repeated — and why, when you look at evidence from someone else's investigation, you should always ask how many times the measurement was repeated.

Questions from the book — 8.3
  1. Marcus and Arun are using acid of pH 1. What should they do to stay safe? Wear safety glasses and take care when handling strong acids. If they spill the acid they should dilute it with water; if they get it on their skin, they should wash it off at once and seek medical help.
  2. Which variables are being kept the same? The volume of acid; the type and strength of the acid; the volume of universal indicator; and the volume of powder added with each spatula.
  3. Which variable is being changed? The powder being tested.
  4. What is being measured? The number of spatulas of powder used to neutralise the acid.
  5. Which is the most effective powder (first set of results)? Powder B.
  6. Which is the least effective powder? Powder C.
  7. Is there enough evidence to be certain? No. There is only one set of results, so there could be mistakes.
  8. After repeating, which powder is the most effective? Powder A.
  9. Which result looks 'wrong'? The first result for powder B.
  10. Suggest why they got this 'wrong' result. They may have miscounted the number of spatulas, or heaped them up so that they were adding more powder each time; or they may have measured the volume of acid incorrectly.
  11. What should they have done about it? Ignored the 'wrong' result and repeated the experiment.
  12. Should the 'wrong' result be included in the mean? No — it should be ignored when calculating the mean.
Think like a scientist — asking questions and planning

In a group, write down four questions about acids and alkalis that you could investigate, then check that each one really can be investigated. Choose one of them and plan how to carry out the investigation, dividing up the tasks — equipment list, method, safety, results table — and share the plan with the class. Self-assessment: was your plan safe, would it work, and was the test fair?

8.4 Detecting chemical reactions

Key words: cloudy · glowing · precipitate

How can you tell a chemical reaction has happened?

In a chemical reaction, new products are formed from the reactants. There are several clues that a reaction has taken place:

  • a gas is given off
  • a reactant seems to 'disappear'
  • there is a colour change
  • heat is produced
  • there is a change in pH
  • a precipitate is formed.

Clue 1: a gas is given off

Reaction 1 — hydrogen. Magnesium reacts with hydrochloric acid and bubbles of hydrogen are given off. Hydrogen burns with a squeaky pop when a lighted splint is placed in the mouth of the tube.

magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen

Reaction 2 — carbon dioxide. When baking powder and vinegar react, carbon dioxide is given off. You test for carbon dioxide using limewater: when carbon dioxide mixes with limewater, the limewater turns cloudy.

Reaction 3 — oxygen. When a piece of apple is placed in hydrogen peroxide, it bubbles and oxygen is given off. You test for oxygen with a glowing splint: if the gas is oxygen, the glowing splint relights.

GasTestPositive result
hydrogenlighted splint in the mouth of the tubesqueaky pop
oxygenglowing splint in the mouth of the tubesplint relights
carbon dioxidebubble the gas through limewaterlimewater turns cloudy

Clue 2: a reactant 'disappears'

When magnesium ribbon reacts with acid, hydrogen is produced and the magnesium ribbon 'disappears'. The magnesium is used up in the reaction: it combines with the chlorine from the hydrochloric acid to form magnesium chloride.

Clue 3: a colour change

Gently heating black copper oxide with sulfuric acid produces a blue solution of copper sulfate.

copper oxide (black) + sulfuric acid → copper sulfate (blue) + water
Safety: do not boil the blue liquid, as harmful fumes will be given off.

Clue 4: heat is produced

When potassium is placed in water, hydrogen is given off and the reaction produces so much heat that the hydrogen burns. (This reaction must only be done by a teacher.) When zinc is added to hydrochloric acid, hydrogen is given off and the test tube feels hot.

Clue 5: a change in pH

When you neutralise an alkali there is a change in pH. This is a neutralisation reaction.

sodium hydroxide + hydrochloric acid → sodium chloride + water

Clue 6: a precipitate is formed

If you mix solutions of silver nitrate and calcium chloride, a solid is formed when the two liquids are mixed. This solid is called a precipitate — here it is silver chloride.

silver nitrate + calcium chloride → silver chloride + calcium nitrate

Limewater is a solution of calcium hydroxide. The limewater turns cloudy when carbon dioxide is bubbled in because a precipitate of calcium carbonate forms — you added a gas to a liquid and a solid was formed.

calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide → calcium carbonate + water
Getting started — 8.4
  • Reactants and products. Reactants are the chemicals you start with in a chemical reaction; products are the chemicals you end up with.
  • Chemical and physical changes. In a chemical change new chemicals are made, as in the reaction between magnesium and hydrochloric acid. In a physical change no new chemicals are formed, but there may be a change of state — for example from a solid to a liquid.
  • Acids and alkalis. An acid has a pH below 7; an alkali has a pH above 7.
Activity 8.4.1 — Testing gases

Testing for carbon dioxide: half-fill a test tube with limewater. Put a small amount of calcium carbonate into another test tube and add hydrochloric acid. Quickly fit the rubber bung and delivery tube, making sure the delivery tube reaches into the limewater.

Testing for oxygen: half-fill a test tube with hydrogen peroxide, add a spatula of manganese dioxide, and place a glowing splint into the neck of the test tube.

  1. What did you see with the limewater? The limewater was colourless to start with. As the carbon dioxide bubbled into the tube, it started to go cloudy; the more gas that was bubbled through, the whiter and cloudier the limewater became.

Workbook — Exercise 8.4B Has a reaction taken place?

One way to tell that a reaction has taken place is that a gas is given off — you see bubbles or fizzing (for example vinegar and baking powder). Three other things to look for:

  1. A colour change. Example: black copper oxide heated with sulfuric acid gives a blue copper sulfate solution.
  2. A change in temperature — heat is produced. Example: zinc added to hydrochloric acid makes the test tube feel hot.
  3. A precipitate forms — a solid appears when two solutions are mixed. Example: silver nitrate mixed with calcium chloride gives a white precipitate of silver chloride.

(A change in pH, or a reactant 'disappearing', would also be accepted.)

Workbook — Exercise 8.4C Testing for gases

You have four test tubes: one contains air, one oxygen, one hydrogen and one carbon dioxide.

Take each tube in turn, keeping your thumb over the mouth until the moment you test it.

  1. Lighted splint. Place a lighted splint in the mouth of the tube. The tube that gives a squeaky pop contains hydrogen.
  2. Glowing splint. Place a glowing splint in the mouth of each of the remaining tubes. The tube in which the splint relights contains oxygen. A splint put into carbon dioxide goes out; in air it keeps glowing but does not relight.
  3. Limewater. To separate carbon dioxide from air, pour a little limewater into each of the last two tubes, put your thumb over the mouth and shake. The limewater that turns cloudy shows the tube contained carbon dioxide; the other tube contained air.

Wear safety glasses throughout.

Project — moving dangerous chemicals

Working in a group of three, write a report as a team of reporters covering a serious road accident involving a truck carrying concentrated acid. Points you could consider:

  • Why is an acid spill so dangerous, and what would happen if people drove through it?
  • How do the emergency services know which chemical they are dealing with (hazard labels and transport documents)?
  • What must they do to the spilt acid, and how will they know when the task is complete (neutralise it, then check the pH)?
  • What safety measures must the emergency services take?
  • What would be the effect of the acid reaching the soil alongside the road?
  • What regulations apply in your area to the transport of dangerous materials, and what extra considerations apply at sea or in the air?

Present your report as a newspaper or magazine article, a radio or television interview, or a class presentation — choose a form you have not used in another science project.
